extracted.intended_audience: college students and young people preparing for careers in newspaper journalism; early-career reporters and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the education, skills, character, and newsroom roles required to prepare for and practice the profession of newspaper making — aimed at students and aspiring newspaper men. Covers preparatory studies, reading lists, practical reporting and editorial skills, and organizational/ethical expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General education and classical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a 'first-class course of general education' and familiarity with Greek, Latin, and older Teutonic languages as foundational to commanding English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaker prefers broad liberal education rather than narrow 'departments of journalism.' Knowing classical languages is said to give command of English 'and all the subtleties and abilities of expression which are in it.' Colleges should give accuracy in learning and fidelity in recitation. Anti-pattern: scattering studies too thinly or pursuing narrow vocational courses at the expense of deep general education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the English language
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough knowledge of English is 'the very cornerstone' of a journalist's education; without it a man 'does not really know the English language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop vocabulary, command of word-resources, and the ability to use language for expression and dissemination of knowledge. This underpins style, clarity, and correctness in reporting and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in observation and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy — 'the faculty of seeing a thing as it is' and being able to state precise quantitative facts (e.g., 'that it is two and one quarter and not two and three eighths').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the 'first and most precious ends of a good education.' Reports must be exact and free from exaggeration or prejudice. Essential across reporting, editing, and editorial responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research skill — knowing where/how to find what you don't know
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability 'to know how and where most promptly to look for what you don't know and what you want to know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes resourcefulness and methodical searching rather than mere memory; crucial for accurate reporting and background for stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, precise reporting without exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'able to tell what you know, and to tell it accurately, precisely, without exaggeration, without prejudice, the fact just as it is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies equally to reporting a baseball game, a sermon, or a lecture; reporters must present facts plainly and honestly. Anti-patterns: sensationalizing, biased wording, or ambiguous accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical faculty / judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivated 'critical faculty' — judgment that can say 'That is true' or 'That is false' quickly and detect error 'without the necessity of any long examination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learned through education and practice; it enables rapid verification and selection of reliable facts or sources. Lack of this faculty leads to conspicuous mistakes even in gifted writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of individual style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style arises from 'the combination of imagination and humor, with the entire command of the word-resources of the language' and distinguishes writers from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style is valuable but partly innate and partly cultivated; cultivate simplicity and clarity rather than imitation. Study great exemplars (Channing, Hawthorne) for instruction, but 'do not take any model' — develop your own natural style and avoid affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imitation and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'labor after' another man's style or imitate mannerisms; avoid affectation and strive for perfect clearness and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitating famous writers (Carlyle, Arnold, etc.) can lead to tedium or mischief. The practical goal is readable, sincere prose suited to the writer's own natural style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of American politics and practical politics
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalist who aspires to 'fill an important place in journalism' must know politics — theory, history, practical workings, the men, their ideas, purposes, and deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest in politics (e.g., reading the political pages) is a sign of suitability. Practical political knowledge helps a journalist play a momentous role in public affairs. Anti-pattern: preference for trivial reading (e.g., only love stories) signals mismatch for general/newspaper journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep understanding of the Constitution(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the Constitution of the United States and state constitutions to understand the principles at the bottom of them — not rote memorization but comprehension of underlying principles and vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding constitutional principles gives perspective beyond ward elections and allows the journalist to see 'clear skies' of political meaning. Knowing state constitutions and the reasons for provisions is important for local responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of history (England, Europe, world)
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity with English history and the history of every European country is needed because the American Constitution and politics are rooted in those traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study origins and causes ('go into the garden where the seed was first sown') to explain present events; history is a 'safe guide' for political action. This is a substantial preparatory course — not all can learn everything at once, but aim for 'something solid.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential reading list for style and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain books are 'absolutely indispensable' to the education of a journalist — notably the Bible, Shakespeare, and Milton (e.g., 'Speech for the Liberty of Unlicensed Printing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bible models 'sublime simplicity' and authoritative expression; Shakespeare is 'the chief master of English speech'; Milton provides high doctrine on press liberty. Read these for style, rhetorical resources, and philosophical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting: factual accuracy, clarity, and liveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must 'learn accurately the facts, and ... state them exactly as they are' and, when possible, add 'a little degree of life, a little approach to eloquence, or a little humor' to make reports strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting is the largest newsroom function; it must be accurate, free from affectation, precise in detail, and may be enhanced by imagination or humor. Example: a gifted but ungrammatical reporter can produce valuable raw material that a scholar-editor polishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational judgment at events
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter is 'the eye of the paper' and must judge the vital facts at an event (e.g., in a fire: which house is greatest, who suffered the greatest loss, whether anyone perished, how it occurred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritization of facts — deciding what is most important and newsworthy at a scene — is essential. This is a learned habit: learn to see the picturesque, interesting, and important aspects quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange-reader / news-selection skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who 'reads the other newspapers and makes extracts from them' must know what should be taken and what is interesting, often reading thousands of papers and judging what to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires judgment, knowledge, experience, a sense of humor, stamina, and the ability to sift huge volumes of material to select items worth reprinting or highlighting. This role is highly important and well-paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript editing and correspondence curation
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor who receives manuscripts must prepare them for press: edit, correct, clarify, fix rhetoric and punctuation, mark paragraphs, and determine whether letters or foreign correspondence should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This role demands literary cultivation and judgment to disentangle twisted facts, improve phrasing, and decide publish-worthiness. Note that large offices often pay for material that is never used; the editor must allocate space and cost wisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist reporting (scientific and technical knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper needs 'a scientific man' who knows electricity, chemistry, and can 'really understand the inventions of Edison' to explain scientific developments correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain beats require specialized cultivation; a generalist cannot adequately cover complex technical subjects without training. This specialization is a department of news of 'supreme consequence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Character, moral integrity, and staying power for leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor-in-chief attains position by natural selection and must combine talent with character — 'the staying power' which is 'not merely intellectual, it is moral.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public trust depends on a leader being believed not to say anything that is not so. Deceptive tactics may have short success but undermine long-term leadership; moral character is central to lasting editorial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of news agencies and synthesis rather than exhaustive collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation of associations and agencies (e.g., the United Press) has lessened the need for every paper to collect all world news; editors can now synthesize agency copy with local reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces drudgery of news-getting, allows editors to focus on intellectual work, and raises the dignity of the profession. Practical implication: learn to integrate wire service material and focus resources where local judgment adds value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical realism about skills vs. talent and earning potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting can be well paid; a reporter's success may depend more on talent (seeing and getting the fact) than on perfect grammar or classical training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: excellent reporters may have poor spelling/grammar yet produce indispensable factual copy that editors polish. Encourage earnestness and sincerity: 'any man who is sincere ... can learn to be a good reporter.'
